papers.title: Enhanced Detection of Recycled FPGAs Using Gaussian Process Regression with LHS and Active Sampling
papers.abstract: Modern Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely utilized across various fields, including artificial intelligence accelerators and Internet of Things (IoT) devices, due to their flexibility and low-cost development potential. However, the problem of “recycled FPGAs” being fraudulently sold as new has grown increasingly severe. This raises significant concerns about reliability degradation caused by performance deterioration, especially in critical applications such as medical and communication systems. Many studies have proposed methods for detecting recycled FPGAs based on delay degradation analysis using Ring Oscillators (ROs). However, the state-of-the-art approach requires a comprehensive evaluation of paths within all lookup tables, leading to increased testing costs and database management overhead. To address this issue, a method combining exhaustive fingerprinting (X-FP) methodology with an advanced RO design is proposed, where a statistical Virtual Probe (VP) model is used to predict the delay of the RO. This research aims to achieve high-accuracy predictions with fewer data points by employing Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) instead of the VP model. This demonstrates that, with actual silicon data, the proposed custom (GPR) improves prediction accuracy by 20% compared with state-of-the-art VP model methods with 50% less training data. The two proposed models demonstrated better performance than Naive GPR, achieving 9% and 7% higher prediction accuracy, respectively. The predictions were further verified using an optimized Autoencoder. The model successfully detected both 10-days and 14-days aged FPGAs among the new ones, achieving 100% overall accuracy using only 10% and 3% training data, respectively. While although the training data predicted by the VP can also detect aged FPGAs, it cannot properly classify all aged and non-aged FPGAs in both 3% and 10% training scenarios. Finally, for further verification in the case of both new and aged FPGA, after prediction, the logistic regression classifier was trained with both old and new FPGA data, achieving 100% correct classification.

papers.title: 30-Day Postoperative Adverse Outcomes: ASA Educational Initiatives Closing Care Gaps
papers.abstract: Over 300 million surgical procedures are performed each year globally.1 An estimated 4 million postoperative deaths occur annually, making it the third leading cause of death both worldwide and within the United States.2,3 Postoperative adverse outcomes including 30-day mortality and unplanned readmission increase health care costs and patient satisfaction and are therefore used as indicators of perioperative quality and safety. These metrics are also used for public reporting and payment-for-performance initiatives.4 Anesthesiologists, as perioperative physicians, and practitioners of pain management, critical care medicine, and palliative medicine, have established themselves as leaders in patient safety and innovation.5 Given their integral involvement across all phases of the perioperative continuum – preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative – they are well positioned to lead initiatives that enhance patient outcomes.6 This article explores the role of education in improving patient care and safety and highlights relevant initiatives from the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA), reviews modern education strategies, and discusses possible education content for teaching and learning aimed at reducing postoperative complications and mortality. Education strategies to address variability and improve outcomes Despite advances in surgical techniques and anesthetic management and implementation of enhanced recovery pathways (ERPs) which have contributed to improved postoperative outcomes, significant variability in perioperative care persists.6 Unwarranted variability and fragmented and uncoordinated care contribute to adverse outcomes.7,8 Factors driving variability include insufficient adherence to best practices, inadequate quality improvement programs, and unconscious bias in clinical decision-making.8 Educational interventions—targeting perioperative care providers, institutional leadership, and patients—play a vital role in improving perioperative care and postoperative outcomes as well as enhancing patient safety and satisfaction. Anesthesiologists can play a vital role in developing and implementing ERPs as well as education of perioperative care providers and hospital/institutional leadership. ASA-led educational initiatives ASA has always been at the forefront of patient safety and perioperative education. ASA offers a wide array of continuing education opportunities aimed at advancing perioperative safety and competence.9 These include flexible, self-paced online modules, webinars, podcasts, and programs such as Anesthesiology Continuing Education (ACE), Summaries of Emerging Evidence (SEE), and Anesthesia Toolbox. One of the innovative tools is Anesthesia SimSTAT, a high-fidelity simulation platform that enables experiential learning in virtual environments. This tool enhances clinical judgment, technical skill, team coordination, and communication—without the need for travel or large simulation centers. ASA also offers certifications in perioperative resuscitation, diagnostic ultrasound, and quality improvement. Additional contributions include the development of evidence-based practice guidelines, analyses from closed claims databases, leadership training, and the Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation (APSF).10 ASA has recently established the Center for Perioperative Medicine (CPMed), which promotes multidisciplinary, patient-centered approaches designed to reduce surgical morbidity and mortality.11 Modern educational approaches Traditional models of continuing medical education are often incompatible with the demanding schedules of clinicians. Also, exponentially expanding volume and variability of scientific knowledge requires a paradigm shift in education programs. Modern approaches focus on interactivity, adaptability, and evidence-based learning strategies that support knowledge retention and clinical application. Modern educational strategies for obtaining knowledge, procedural skills, and professionalism should be accessible, time-efficient, contextually relevant, and tailored to real-world practice. Modern technology can be used to facilitate self-directed active learning through webinars and podcasts and offers greater flexibility in terms of time and accessibility.12 Cognitive aids are critical during clinical crises as they bridge knowledge gaps. Other educational methods include e-learning, spaced learning, interleaving, retrieval practice, experiential learning, feedback from multiple sources, and microlearning formats that deliver targeted information in brief segments.13 Online forums and social media allow networking, self-learning, and global collaboration. Simulation-based education remains a cornerstone of skill development. It enables both technical and nontechnical training in a safe environment and fosters long-term memory retention through simulated stress responses. Newer tools, such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR), offer immersive training with three-dimensional visualization.14 VR is particularly beneficial for simulating unfamiliar scenarios and provides a cost-effective alternative to traditional simulators. AR enhances real-time training by overlaying holographic content in real-world settings, making it useful for procedural training and team communication. Each technology has unique strengths and limitations in terms of realism, scope, and cost. Virtual game-based learning, including activities such as “Jeopardy” and quiz competitions, promotes engagement and knowledge consolidation. Game simulations allow hands-on practice in responding to challenges without expensive physical simulators. Of note, educational interventions that are project-based efforts without long-term support lack sustainability.Table 1: Educational methodologies based on domains of utilization. Anesthesiology 2019;131(4):908-28.Designing a perioperative education curriculum An effective educational curriculum should be evidence-driven, pragmatic, and customized to accommodate variability in local practices as well as address global disparities in perioperative care. Curriculum content on postoperative morbidity and mortality should include information on incidence, risk factors, predictive tools to identify high-risk patients, and interventions to improve patient outcomes. Education should be aimed at health care professionals involved with perioperative care (anesthesiologists, surgeons, nurses, etc.) as well as patients. Risk stratification tools such as Surgical Outcome Risk Tool (SORT),15 Surgical Risk Scale,16 and frailty assessment should be emphasized over subjective clinical assessments. Risk prediction tools allow better resource utilization, while improving perioperative outcomes. In addition, education should include preoperative optimization of comorbid conditions and prehabilitation, optimal intraoperative management, and postoperative disposition including admission to the critical care unit or enhanced postoperative monitoring on the hospital ward.Table 2: Sampling of educational tools specific to anesthesiology learners. Education would address causes of readmission, including care transition and socioeconomic issues. Postdischarge bundled interventions that combine personalized discharge instructions with early follow-up have been shown to reduce hospital readmission. Team-based training is another essential component because fragmented care and poor transition of care contribute to postoperative adverse events. Training should encourage multidisciplinary collaboration and communication as well as an approach to utilization of escalation protocols to promote timely recognition of patient deterioration and improve team decision-making.17 Increasing familiarity of the surgeon-anesthesiologist dyad has been reported to improve postoperative outcomes.18 Educational programs that facilitate implementation of ERP and focus on the continuum of care by improving communication, protocol adherence, and team-based care have demonstrated meaningful improvements in surgical outcomes. Customizing care that recognizes that each patient is different and may have different needs and preferences is essential to ensure equitable access to life-saving surgical care. Nurse education Perioperative nurses play a pivotal role in executing ERPs and reducing variability. Nurse education programs should focus on early recognition of complications, appropriate escalation of care, and communication strategies. Enhanced nursing education is associated with lower failure-to-rescue rates and improved patient survival. Patient education Health literacy is imperative for ensuring a smooth surgical recovery process. Therefore, educational programs are necessary to improve patients' understanding and health literacy with regard to managing their preoperative preparation and postoperative recovery.19,20 Educational content should be culturally sensitive, linguistically appropriate, and tailored to diverse literacy levels. Education modules may include preoperative medication management, signs of complications, and the importance of follow-up care. Encouraging patient participation in shared decision-making enhances safety and satisfaction. Implementation challenges Despite the benefits, several obstacles hinder the widespread adoption of educational interventions. These include resource constraints (e.g., lack of infrastructure, trained educators, and financial resources), lack of institutional support, limited access to academic resources (e.g., practitioners in rural or private settings), and cultural factors such as hierarchical environments that limit protocol-driven practices. Other barriers include information overload, variability in educational content quality most likely due to lack of evidence, and difficulty distinguishing clinically relevant information from background noise (i.e., filtering and applying evidence-based knowledge). There must be emphasis on addressing the “knowing-doing gap” wherein the practitioners may have the knowledge but do not or cannot implement this knowledge in clinical practice. It is necessary to understand the benefits and limitations of the various education types. In summary, comprehensive educational programs targeting perioperative care providers (physicians and nurses), institutional leadership, and patients are fundamental to improving surgical outcomes and patient safety. Anesthesiologists are uniquely positioned to lead these efforts. ASA remains at the forefront of offering state-of-the-art education geared towards improving patient safety and patient care. Education should be tailored to busy clinicians – enable lifelong learning through scalable, accessible, and effective strategies. The educational content must be clinically relevant, outcomes-focused, and frequently updated. Also, the impact of education interventions on patient outcomes should be evaluated, although this could be challenging because of multifactorial influences on patient outcomes. Finally, continued research, sustained investment, and collaborative development of educational programs are essential to advancing perioperative quality and reducing postoperative mortality.
